--- title: "Reshaping and aggregation" subtitle: "Session 8 · Topic 2.6 · Thu 17 Dec" format: revealjs --- ## Today ::: {.agenda} 1. Group and summarise: `groupby` + `agg` 2. Turning continuous inputs into classes: `cut`, `qcut` 3. Pivot tables and cross-tabulations 4. Wide and long format: `melt`, `pivot` 5. Combining tables: `concat`, `merge` ::: ## Setup for today ::: {#dd440a25 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import numpy as np df = pd.read_csv("data/bracket.csv") ``` ::: ## Split – apply – combine Question: *how does the mean stress depend on the thickness class?* ``` split by class apply mean combine 8–12 mm → rows … → mean ┐ 12–16 mm → rows … → mean ├→ one small table 16–20 mm → rows … → mean ┘ ``` That is `groupby`. # Grouping {.divider} ## Classes from continuous values: `cut` ::: {#e6612d6d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["t_class"] = pd.cut(df["thickness_mm"], bins=[8, 12, 16, 20], labels=["8–12", "12–16", "16–20"], include_lowest=True) df["t_class"].value_counts().sort_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` t_class 8–12 110 12–16 94 16–20 96 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: - `pd.cut` — fixed boundaries you choose (engineering classes) - `pd.qcut(col, 4)` — quartiles: equal number of runs per class ## `groupby` + one statistic ::: {#aeed1bca .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.groupby("t_class", observed=True)["max_stress_MPa"].mean().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` t_class 8–12 566.9 12–16 282.5 16–20 190.2 Name: max_stress_MPa, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#dd1dacd9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.groupby("t_class", observed=True)[["max_stress_MPa", "deflection_mm"]].median().round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
max_stress_MPa deflection_mm
t_class
8–12 565.00 2.87
12–16 249.85 0.90
16–20 185.60 0.48
``` ::: ::: ## `agg`: several statistics at once ::: {#db75ed34 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} summary = df.groupby("t_class", observed=True).agg( runs=("run_id", "count"), stress_mean=("max_stress_MPa", "mean"), stress_max=("max_stress_MPa", "max"), sf_min=("safety_factor", "min"), share_failed=("safety_factor", lambda s: (s < 1).mean()), ).round(2) summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
runs stress_mean stress_max sf_min share_failed
t_class
8–12 110 566.93 1443.1 0.25 0.72
12–16 94 282.48 735.6 0.48 0.35
16–20 96 190.22 469.8 0.76 0.06
``` ::: ::: - named aggregation: `new_name=("column", "function")` - functions: `"count"`, `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"std"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"sum"`, or your own ## Grouping by two variables ::: {#1694b7aa .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["r_class"] = pd.cut(df["fillet_radius_mm"], [1, 3, 5.5, 8], labels=["small r", "medium r", "large r"], include_lowest=True) two = df.groupby(["t_class", "r_class"], observed=True)["max_stress_MPa"].mean().round(0) two ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` t_class r_class 8–12 small r 707.0 medium r 578.0 large r 420.0 12–16 small r 352.0 medium r 276.0 large r 243.0 16–20 small r 249.0 medium r 184.0 large r 148.0 Name: max_stress_MPa, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: - the result has a **two-level index** — hard to read; a pivot table is better ↓ # Pivot tables {.divider} ## `pivot_table` ::: {#06a40051 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.pivot_table(df, values="max_stress_MPa", index="t_class", columns="r_class", aggfunc="mean", observed=True).round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
r_class small r medium r large r
t_class
8–12 707.0 578.0 420.0
12–16 352.0 276.0 243.0
16–20 249.0 184.0 148.0
``` ::: ::: - like a pivot table in Excel: rows × columns, one aggregated value - `.unstack()` turns the two-level result from the previous slide into the same table ## Counting combinations: `crosstab` ::: {#859db126 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["verdict"] = np.where(df["safety_factor"] >= 1.5, "pass", "fail") pd.crosstab(df["t_class"], df["verdict"], margins=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
verdict fail pass All
t_class
8–12 89 21 110
12–16 52 42 94
16–20 38 58 96
All 179 121 300
``` ::: ::: ## Shares instead of counts ::: {#898cd0ed .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.crosstab(df["t_class"], df["verdict"], normalize="index").round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
verdict fail pass
t_class
8–12 0.81 0.19
12–16 0.55 0.45
16–20 0.40 0.60
``` ::: ::: ::: {.tip} Crosstab of a design-space cell vs. verdict also shows **coverage**: a cell with 2 runs tells you little. Remember this when a model is "bad" in one region. ::: # Wide and long format {.divider} ## The same data, two shapes ::: {#f8d7e215 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} wide = pd.read_csv("data/bracket_loadcases.csv") wide.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
run_id thickness_mm fillet_radius_mm stress_LC1_static stress_LC2_impact stress_LC3_lateral
0 R001 17.3 6.5 170.4 238.6 324.5
1 R002 13.3 1.9 527.5 738.5 677.0
2 R003 18.3 4.8 297.9 417.1 617.1
``` ::: ::: - **wide**: one row per run, one column per load case — easy to read - **long**: one row per run *and* load case — easy to group, filter and plot ## `melt`: wide → long ::: {#880741c0 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} long = wide.melt( id_vars=["run_id", "thickness_mm", "fillet_radius_mm"], var_name="load_case", value_name="stress_MPa", ) long["load_case"] = long["load_case"].str.replace("stress_", "") long.sort_values("run_id").head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
run_id thickness_mm fillet_radius_mm load_case stress_MPa
0 R001 17.3 6.5 LC1_static 170.4
60 R001 17.3 6.5 LC2_impact 238.6
120 R001 17.3 6.5 LC3_lateral 324.5
1 R002 13.3 1.9 LC1_static 527.5
61 R002 13.3 1.9 LC2_impact 738.5
121 R002 13.3 1.9 LC3_lateral 677.0
``` ::: ::: ## Now grouping is easy ::: {#83dbd045 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} long.groupby("load_case")["stress_MPa"].agg(["mean", "max"]).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
mean max
load_case
LC1_static 350.6 1443.1
LC2_impact 490.8 2020.3
LC3_lateral 442.2 880.3
``` ::: ::: ::: {#ecdbf35b .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} governing = long.loc[long.groupby("run_id")["stress_MPa"].idxmax()] governing["load_case"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` load_case LC3_lateral 30 LC2_impact 30 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: - `idxmax` per group → the **governing load case** for each run ## `pivot`: long → wide ::: {#3d87059c .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} back = long.pivot(index="run_id", columns="load_case", values="stress_MPa") back.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
load_case LC1_static LC2_impact LC3_lateral
run_id
R001 170.4 238.6 324.5
R002 527.5 738.5 677.0
R003 297.9 417.1 617.1
``` ::: ::: - `pivot` needs unique (index, column) pairs; otherwise use `pivot_table` with an `aggfunc` # Combining tables {.divider} ## `concat`: stack tables with the same columns ::: {#b9e25985 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} batch1 = df.iloc[:150] batch2 = df.iloc[150:] all_runs = pd.concat([batch1, batch2], ignore_index=True) print(len(batch1), len(batch2), len(all_runs)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 150 150 300 ``` ::: ::: - typical: results from several solver batches, several days, several colleagues - check afterwards: are IDs still unique? ## `merge`: join by a key ::: {#4c7ccaf5 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} materials = pd.read_csv("data/materials.csv") materials ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
material yield_MPa
0 S235 235
1 S355 355
2 S460 460
``` ::: ::: ::: {#75c4d11b .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} design = pd.DataFrame({"run_id": ["R001", "R002", "R003"], "material": ["S355", "S235", "S460"]}) merged = (design .merge(df[["run_id", "max_stress_MPa"]], on="run_id", how="left") .merge(materials, on="material", how="left")) merged["sf"] = merged["yield_MPa"] / merged["max_stress_MPa"] merged.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
run_id material max_stress_MPa yield_MPa sf
0 R001 S355 170.4 355 2.08
1 R002 S235 527.5 235 0.45
2 R003 S460 297.9 460 1.54
``` ::: ::: ## Join types | `how=` | keeps | |---|---| | `"inner"` | only keys present in **both** tables | | `"left"` | all rows of the left table; missing matches → `NaN` | | `"outer"` | all keys from both | | `"cross"` | every row with every row (all combinations) | ::: {#574c1dee .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} check = df.merge(materials, how="cross") check["sf"] = check["yield_MPa"] / check["max_stress_MPa"] pd.crosstab(check["material"], check["sf"] >= 1.5, normalize="index").round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ```{=html}
sf False True
material
S235 0.73 0.27
S355 0.60 0.40
S460 0.46 0.54
``` ::: ::: ::: {.muted} After a merge, always compare the number of rows before and after. Unexpected growth = duplicate keys. ::: ## Your turn (30 min) ::: {.exercise} 1. Classify load into 3 classes with `pd.qcut`. For each load class × thickness class: number of runs, mean stress, share of runs with SF < 1.5 (one `pivot_table` per statistic). 2. From `bracket_loadcases.csv`: melt to long format, find the governing load case per run, and its safety factor for S355. 3. Using a `"cross"` merge with `materials.csv`: for every run, which is the **cheapest** steel grade (lowest yield) that gives SF ≥ 1.5? How many runs need S460? How many cannot be saved by any grade? ::: ## Summary - `pd.cut` / `pd.qcut` — classes from continuous variables - `groupby(...).agg(name=(col, func))` — split, apply, combine - `pivot_table` and `crosstab` — two-way summaries - `melt` (wide → long) and `pivot` (long → wide) - `concat` stacks, `merge` joins by keys; check row counts after every merge **After the break (Tue 13 Jan):** exploratory data analysis — asking the data questions systematically. ## Practice at home (~1 h) - finish exercise 3 and commit - think of a question about your own calculations that needs a `groupby` — write it down ## Over the break ::: {.muted} No obligatory homework. If you want to practise: ::: - load a table from your own work (CSV or Excel) with pandas, clean it and summarise it with `groupby` - write down anything that went wrong — we start Session 9 with a recap and your examples
